lessons.title: Designing a Rodent-Proof Hay Store
lessons.body:
Rodents can destroy up to 30% of your stored hay. To stop them, you need a store that rats and mice cannot enter. The cheapest effective design is a raised platform store. Build a wooden or metal frame that lifts the hay at least 60 cm off the ground. Cover the legs with smooth metal cones or empty tin cans â rodents cannot climb past these. The floor should be made of tight-fitting planks or metal sheets, not mud or loose soil. Walls can be made of mud bricks, but plaster them smooth and fill any cracks larger than 6 mm. The roof should overhang by at least 45 cm to keep rain off the walls. Use galvanized iron sheets or thatch, but ensure no gaps at the eaves.

Inside the store, keep hay on pallets or a second raised floor of poles spaced no more than 5 cm apart. This allows air to circulate and prevents rodents from nesting under the bales. Store bales in tight stacks, but leave a 30 cm gap between the stack and the walls for inspection. Check for rodent droppings, gnaw marks, or burrows every week. If you find signs, set traps or use cats. Never use poison inside a hay store â it can contaminate the feed.

For a small farm, a simple metal bin with a tight lid works well. For larger quantities, a brick store with a concrete floor and metal door is best. The door should fit tightly and have a metal kick plate at the bottom. Seal any pipes or wires entering the store with wire mesh. Remember, a rodent-proof store also keeps out birds and insects. The cost of building a good store is far less than the hay you will lose. In Africa, many farmers use locally available materials like bamboo, mud, and thatch, but always reinforce with metal where rodents can chew. A well-designed store can last 10 years and save you money every season.

lessons.title: Protecting Silage from Rain and Sun
lessons.body:
Silage is wet feed that ferments without air. Rain and sun can ruin it quickly. Rain adds water, which causes mold and rot. Sun dries the silage, stopping fermentation and turning it into poor hay. To protect silage, you must cover it completely. The best cover is a thick plastic silage tarpaulin, but many farmers use local materials like banana leaves, palm fronds, or old maize sacks. Whatever you use, the cover must be airtight and weighted down.

For a pit silo, fill it with chopped forage, pack it tightly to remove air, then cover with a plastic sheet that overlaps the edges by at least 1 meter. On top of the plastic, spread a 15 cm layer of soil or sand. This keeps the plastic pressed down and blocks sunlight. For a bunker silo, use a plastic sheet and then old tires every 2 meters to hold it down. Never use black plastic that has been in the sun for more than 6 months â it becomes brittle and cracks. In hot African climates, silage can overheat if exposed to sun. A reflective cover (white or silver) is better than black.

If you use local mats, make sure they are tightly woven and layered at least 5 cm thick. Soak them in water before use to make them swell and seal gaps. After covering, check the silo daily for the first week. If you see holes or tears, patch them with tape or more plastic. Rainwater must not pool on the cover â slope the top so water runs off. Also, keep the area around the silo free of tall grass and debris, which can harbor pests and block airflow. During the rainy season, build a small roof over the silo if possible. A simple thatch roof on poles will keep off direct rain and reduce sun damage. Remember, silage that gets wet will smell like vinegar or rot. If that happens, remove the spoiled layer and feed it to cattle immediately â do not store it. Proper covering is the difference between sweet-smelling silage and a wasted harvest.

lessons.title: Using Tarpaulins and Local Mats for Covering
lessons.body:
Tarpaulins are the most reliable cover for hay and silage, but they can be expensive. In Africa, you can buy UV-resistant plastic tarps in sizes like 4m x 6m or 6m x 10m. A good tarp lasts 2-3 years if cared for. When buying, choose a heavy-duty tarp (at least 200 g/mÂ²) with metal grommets every 50 cm. For hay, place the tarp directly on top of the stack and tie it down with ropes through the grommets. For silage, use a tarp that is at least 0.15 mm thick â thin ones tear easily. Always overlap tarps by at least 1 meter and seal the seam with tape or by folding.

If you cannot afford a tarp, local mats are a good alternative. Woven grass mats, palm frond mats, or even old rice sacks sewn together can work. Make them at least 2 cm thick and 2m x 3m in size. Lay them like roof tiles, starting from the bottom and overlapping upwards by 30 cm. This sheds water. Soak mats in water before use to make them swell and close gaps. After laying, cover the mats with a layer of banana leaves or plastic sheeting to improve waterproofing. Weigh everything down with stones, logs, or old tires. Check mats every week â they rot in damp conditions. Replace any that are torn or moldy.

For both tarps and mats, the key is to keep the cover tight and dry. After rain, remove any standing water by sweeping or using a pump. If water pools, it will seep through. In windy areas, tie ropes across the cover in a crisscross pattern. For silage, you can also use a layer of molasses or salt on top of the silage before covering â this discourages mold. Never use a cover that has been contaminated with oil, diesel, or chemicals. Store your tarps and mats in a dry, shaded place when not in use. Roll them, do not fold, to prevent cracks. With good care, a tarp can last many seasons, and local mats can be made fresh each year. The goal is simple: keep water out and keep the feed dry.

lessons.title: Managing Temperature and Ventilation in Storage
lessons.body:
Temperature and ventilation are critical for both hay and silage. Hay that is too hot can catch fire. Silage that is too hot loses nutrients. For hay, the ideal moisture content for storage is 15-20%. If hay is baled wetter than 20%, it will heat up. Check temperature by pushing a metal rod into the stack and leaving it for 20 minutes. If the rod is too hot to hold, the hay is overheating. In that case, take the stack apart and dry it in the sun. For long-term storage, keep hay in a ventilated shed. Air must move through the bales. Stack bales on their sides with gaps of 10 cm between rows. Do not stack against walls. Leave a 30 cm gap. In hot African climates, a roof with vents or a ridge gap allows hot air to escape. A simple thatch roof with an open ridge works well.

For silage, temperature should stay below 30Â°C. If it rises above 40Â°C, you have too much air in the silo. This happens if the silage is not packed tightly or if the cover leaks. To fix it, add more weight on the cover and seal any holes. For bunker silos, roll the cover tightly and use more tires. For pit silos, add more soil on top. Ventilation for silage is different â you want no air. But you need to let gases escape during fermentation. A one-way valve or a small hole covered with a plastic flap can work. After fermentation stops (about 3 weeks), seal the hole.

In storage, monitor temperature weekly. Use a long thermometer or a metal rod. If hay reaches 60Â°C, it is dangerous â remove it. If silage reaches 45Â°C, feed it quickly. Proper ventilation for hay means air in, moisture out. For silage, it means air out, no air in. In Africa, many farmers store hay in open sheds with good airflow. For silage, keep it in the shade to avoid sun heating. A well-managed store will keep feed cool and dry. Remember, heat is the enemy of quality. Check your store every week, and act fast if temperatures rise.

lessons.title: Preventing Theft and Animal Damage
lessons.body:
Theft and animal damage can wipe out your stored feed. In many African communities, hay and silage are valuable, especially in the dry season. To prevent theft, start with a good fence. A thorny hedge like sisal or acacia works well, but a chain-link fence 2 meters high is better. Add a lockable gate. If you store feed in a shed, use a strong padlock and keep the key with only trusted family members. For silage pits, cover them with heavy stones or logs that are hard to move. You can also mark your bales with paint or a brand to identify them if stolen. Work with neighbors to watch each other's stores. A community watch can reduce theft significantly.

Animal damage is more common. Rodents, birds, and even livestock can ruin feed. For rodents, follow the rodent-proof store design. For birds, cover hay with a tarp or netting. For larger animals like goats or cattle, build a strong fence. If animals break in, they will eat and trample the feed. Also, keep dogs to scare away wild animals. In some areas, elephants or monkeys raid stores. For these, you need a solid building with metal doors and no gaps. Electric fencing is effective but expensive. A simpler method is to hang noisy objects like tin cans on strings around the store â the noise scares animals.

Inside the store, keep feed off the ground. Use pallets or raised platforms. This prevents dampness and makes it harder for rodents. Store hay in tight bales and silage in sealed containers. Check for signs of damage every week: droppings, gnaw marks, footprints, or torn covers. If you find damage, repair it immediately. For theft, consider storing small amounts in your house. For large amounts, a secure barn is best. In Africa, many farmers use a combination of fences, locks, and community vigilance. Never leave a store unlocked. Even a simple rope tied across the door can show if someone entered. Remember, your feed is your wealth. Protect it like you protect your money.

lessons.title: Inventory Management for Year-Round Supply
lessons.body:
Inventory management means knowing how much feed you have and how long it will last. Without a plan, you may run out in the dry season or feed too much and waste. Start by estimating your animals' needs. A mature cow eats about 2.5% of its body weight in dry matter per day. A 400 kg cow needs 10 kg of hay or silage per day. If you have 10 cows, that is 100 kg per day. Over 6 months (180 days), you need 18,000 kg (18 tonnes). If a bale weighs 20 kg, you need 900 bales. For silage, 1 cubic meter of silage weighs about 600 kg. So you need 30 cubic meters for 10 cows for 6 months.

Once you know your needs, measure your store. Count bales or estimate silage volume. Write it down. Use a simple notebook or a chalkboard. Record the date you stored each batch. Then, each week, record how much you feed. Subtract from your total. This tells you how many days of feed remain. If you have less than 30 days left before the next harvest, you need to buy or ration. Rationing means feeding less and supplementing with crop residues or concentrates. For example, mix hay with maize stover or cotton seed cake. This stretches your supply.

Also, rotate your stock. Use the oldest feed first. Hay and silage lose quality over time. Hay stored for more than a year becomes dusty and less nutritious. Silage can last 2-3 years if sealed, but after opening, use it within 2 weeks. Keep a chart on the wall. Mark when you open a new silo or stack. For silage, once you open a pit, you must feed from it daily until it is finished, or it will spoil. So plan to open only what you can use in a short time. If you have multiple pits, open one at a time. For hay, keep bales in a dry place and check for mold. In Africa, many farmers lose feed because they do not track it. A simple inventory can save you from hunger. Teach your family to record feed use. At the end of the season, review your records. How much did you use? How much was wasted? Adjust next year. Good inventory means your animals eat well all year.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Storage and Preservation of Silage and Hay

Storage is where money is either protected or lost. A well-made silage pit or hay bale that is badly stored can lose 20â40% of its feed value within a single season â through rodent contamination, rain damage, mould, theft, or simple spoilage. For African smallholder and emerging commercial farmers, the storage structure is often the cheapest intervention with the highest return. This lesson gives you the practical specifications, costs, and management routines to store silage and hay so that every tonne you harvested reaches the animal, not the rats.

The diagram above is the reference design for a combined hay and silage store. Every element â the raised floor, the mesh skirt, the roof overhang, the ridge ventilation gap, the separation between hay and silage â exists to solve a specific loss problem. Build it once, and you protect feed for years.

Designing a Rodent-Proof Hay Store

Rodents (rats, mice, and in some regions cane rats) are the single largest cause of dry-matter loss in stored hay in sub-Saharan Africa. A rat colony of 20 animals can consume or contaminate 1â2 kg of hay per day â that is over 400 kg per year, worth roughly USD 80â150 at local market prices. The design principles are simple:

  • Raise the floor 100â150 mm above ground on a concrete or stone plinth. Rats cannot tunnel into a raised, hard-edged floor.
  • Fit a galvanised wire mesh skirt (6 mm aperture) around the base, extending 300 mm up the wall and 100 mm outward on the ground.
  • Keep bales 100 mm away from walls so rats cannot run behind them undetected.
  • Clear a 1 m vegetation-free zone around the store â no grass, no rubbish, no hiding cover.
  • Use metal or concrete posts, not timber, for the main structure. Timber posts are rat highways.

Protecting Silage from Rain and Sun

Silage spoils differently from hay. The enemy is oxygen and water ingress, not just rodents. A silage bunker or pit must be sealed within 24â48 hours of filling. Rain entering the top of an open bunker creates a wet, mouldy layer that can spoil 150â300 mm of silage across the entire surface. Sun exposure degrades the plastic cover and causes surface heating, which encourages aerobic spoilage.

The rule is: cover, seal, weight. Cover with a UV-stabilised silage tarpaulin (200â250 micron minimum), seal the edges with soil or sandbags, and weight the entire surface with tyres, sandbags, or a continuous soil layer. In West Africa, many farmers use a 100 mm layer of compacted soil over the plastic â it is cheap, effective, and doubles as a rain shield.

Using Tarpaulins and Local Mats for Covering

Imported silage tarpaulins cost USD 40â120 depending on size, but they last 3â5 seasons if handled carefully. Local alternatives include:

  • Woven polypropylene sacks stitched into large sheets â cheap, but degrade in 1â2 seasons under UV.
  • Thatch mats (grass or palm) laid over plastic sheeting â the thatch takes the UV damage, the plastic keeps the seal.
  • Old maize stalk mats â useful as a sacrificial top layer, not as a primary seal.

The key business point: a tarpaulin that costs USD 80 and lasts 4 seasons protects silage worth USD 2,000â5,000 per season. The return on investment is enormous. Do not substitute a cheap plastic sheet that tears in the first wind.

Managing Temperature and Ventilation in Storage

Hay should be stored at below 15% moisture. If hay is baled at 20â25% moisture, internal heating can reach 60â70Â°C within days, causing spontaneous combustion and total loss. The rule: if you can smell caramel or see steam, the stack is overheating â break it open immediately.

Silage, by contrast, needs anaerobic conditions. Temperature should stabilise at 25â35Â°C after fermentation. If the silage face is warm to the touch (above 40Â°C), aerobic spoilage has begun. Feed off the face quickly, keep the face tight, and never leave loose silage exposed overnight.

Table 1: Storage conditions and expected losses for hay and silage in tropical African conditions
Parameter Hay (dry) Silage (ensiled)
Target moisture at storage 12â15% 65â70%
Temperature range Ambient, below 30Â°C 25â35Â°C (fermentation)
Ventilation requirement Good air movement None â anaerobic seal
Typical dry-matter loss (well managed) 5â10% 8â15%
Typical dry-matter loss (poor storage) 25â40% 20â35%
Main spoilage agents Rain, rodents, mould Air, rain, surface mould

Source: Adapted from FAO, Hay and silage making (2014); ILRI, Feed storage in smallholder systems (2018).

Preventing Theft and Animal Damage

In many African farming contexts, theft of stored feed â especially during the dry season when prices peak â is a real and under-reported loss. So is damage by livestock, dogs, and wildlife. Practical measures:

  • Lockable door or gate on the store, even if it is a simple padlock and chain.
  • Store within sight of the homestead or in a compound with night-time presence.
  • Fence the store perimeter with thorn bush, wire, or live fence (e.g. Euphorbia tirucalli).
  • Mark bales with paint or branded tags so stolen bales can be identified.
  • Record every removal â a simple notebook prevents internal "leakage" as much as external theft.

Inventory Management for Year-Round Supply

The business logic of storage is simple: feed harvested in the wet season must carry the herd through the dry season. If you do not know how much you have, you cannot plan. A basic inventory system requires only a notebook and a monthly count.

Calculate your daily feed requirement: a 400 kg cow eats roughly 10â12 kg of hay equivalent per day. A herd of 10 cows therefore needs 100â120 kg per day, or about 3â3.6 tonnes per month. Over a 5-month dry season, that is 15â18 tonnes. If your store holds 12 tonnes, you have a 3â6 tonne gap â either buy supplementary feed or reduce the herd.

Table 2: Indicative storage capacity and cost for a 10-cow herd (5-month dry season)
Item Quantity / Size Indicative cost (USD) Notes
Hay required 15â18 tonnes â At 10â12 kg/cow/day
Store footprint 6 m Ã 4 m Ã 3 m â Holds ~18â20 tonnes baled hay
Roof (corrugated iron) 30 mÂ² 250â400 Local supplier, includes fixings
Raised floor (timber + plinth) 24 mÂ² 150â300 Concrete plinth preferred
Wire mesh skirt 20 m Ã 0.4 m 40â80 6 mm galvanised
Silage tarpaulin 6 m Ã 8 m, 200 micron 80â120 UV-stabilised, 3â5 seasons
Padlock, chain, fittings â 20â40 â
Total capital â 540â940 Protects feed worth 2,000â5,000/season

Source: Cost ranges compiled from ILRI Feed Storage Guidelines (2018), FAO Smallholder Silage Manual (2014), and regional agri-input supplier quotes in Kenya, Tanzania, and Ghana (2023â2024).

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Spontaneous Combustion and Suffocation

Hay baled above 20% moisture can heat internally and ignite spontaneously â often within 3â6 weeks of storage. Never enter a hay store that is warm to the touch, smells of caramel or burning, or shows steam. Open the doors from outside and call the fire service. Separately, silage pits and sealed bunkers can accumulate carbon dioxide and other gases. Never enter a sealed silage pit or an enclosed silage store without forced ventilation and a second person present. Gas can kill in seconds.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Floor raised 100â150 mm on concrete or stone plinth â no direct ground contact.
  2. Wire mesh skirt (6 mm) fitted around the base, 300 mm up and 100 mm out.
  3. Roof overhang 300 mm on all sides; ridge ventilation gap open.
  4. Bales stacked 100 mm off walls; no vegetation within 1 m of store.
  5. Hay moisture below 15% before baling; smell test for caramel = danger.
  6. Silage sealed within 48 hours; tarpaulin weighted with tyres or soil.
  7. Lockable door + monthly inventory count recorded in a notebook.
  8. Daily feed requirement calculated against stored tonnage â know your gap before the dry season starts.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Hay and Silage Making: A Guide for Smallholder Farmers (free PDF)
  • ILRI â Feed Storage and Preservation in Smallholder Systems (free repository access)
  • FAO â Tropical Silage Production and Utilisation (free online)
  • Kenya Ministry of Agriculture â Fodder Conservation Guidelines (free download)
  • CIMMYT â Conservation Agriculture and Fodder Storage (free publications)

Business bottom line: A well-built store costs USD 500â900 and protects feed worth USD 2,000â5,000 every season. The payback period is one dry season. Farmers who store well sell surplus feed at peak prices; farmers who store poorly buy replacement feed at peak prices. The structure is the difference between a cost centre and a profit centre.

quiz.q: What is the minimum height above ground for a rodent-proof hay store platform?
quiz.explanation: Raising hay at least 60 cm off the ground helps prevent rodents from climbing into the store.

quiz.q: Which material is best for covering a silage pit to make it airtight?
quiz.explanation: A thick plastic tarpaulin provides an airtight seal, which is essential for proper silage fermentation.

quiz.q: How often should you check a silo cover for holes or tears during the first week?
quiz.explanation: Daily checks in the first week allow you to quickly repair any damage and prevent spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for hay to be stored safely?
quiz.explanation: Hay with 15-20% moisture is dry enough to prevent heating and mold growth during storage.

quiz.q: What temperature indicates that hay is overheating and may catch fire?
quiz.explanation: Hay reaching 60Â°C is dangerously hot and must be removed to prevent spontaneous combustion.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of ventilation in a hay store?
options: A) To keep the hay warm
B) To allow air to move and remove moisture
quiz.explanation: Ventilation allows air to circulate, removing moisture and preventing mold and heating.

quiz.q: How can you prevent rodents from climbing the legs of a raised hay store?
options: B) Wrap legs with smooth metal cones
C) Put water around the legs
quiz.explanation: Smooth metal cones or tin cans create a slippery barrier that rodents cannot climb.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find moldy silage when you open a pit?
options: A) Mix it with good silage
B) Feed it to cattle immediately
C) Remove the spoiled layer and discard it
D) Dry it in the sun
quiz.explanation: Moldy silage can be toxic; remove and discard the spoiled portion to keep the rest safe.

quiz.q: Which type of cover is best for reflecting sunlight and reducing heat in silage storage?
options: B) White or silver reflective cover
quiz.explanation: A white or silver cover reflects sunlight, keeping the silage cooler and reducing heat damage.

quiz.q: How often should you check stored feed for signs of theft or animal damage?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks help you detect and address problems before they cause major losses.

quiz.q: What is a good local material to use as a cover for silage if you cannot afford a tarpaulin?
quiz.explanation: Woven grass mats, when layered thickly and soaked, can provide a decent airtight cover.

quiz.q: How much dry matter does a 400 kg cow eat per day?
quiz.explanation: A cow eats about 2.5% of its body weight in dry matter, so 400 kg x 0.025 = 10 kg.

quiz.q: What is the weight of 1 cubic meter of silage?
quiz.explanation: One cubic meter of well-packed silage weighs approximately 600 kg.

quiz.q: Why should you rotate your feed stock and use the oldest first?
options: B) To prevent spoilage and maintain quality
quiz.explanation: Older feed loses quality over time, so using it first prevents waste and maintains nutritional value.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to record feed inventory?
quiz.explanation: A notebook or chalkboard is a low-cost, practical way to track feed amounts and usage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have less than 30 days of feed left before the next harvest?
options: A) Feed more to finish it
quiz.explanation: Rationing or buying feed ensures your animals have enough until the next harvest.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of rodent damage in a hay store?
quiz.explanation: Gnaw marks and droppings are clear indicators that rodents are present and damaging the feed.

quiz.q: How can you protect stored feed from birds?
options: A) Use a tarp or netting
quiz.explanation: Covering hay with a tarp or netting physically blocks birds from accessing the feed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended overlap when laying tarps or mats on a silage pit?
quiz.explanation: A 1-meter overlap ensures a good seal and prevents water from seeping between layers.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using poison inside a hay store?
options: B) It can contaminate the feed
quiz.explanation: Poison can contaminate hay or silage, making it unsafe for livestock to eat.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store hay bales to allow air circulation?
options: B) Stack on their sides with gaps
quiz.explanation: Stacking bales on their sides with gaps allows air to move through and dry the hay.

quiz.q: What should you do if the temperature of stored silage rises above 40Â°C?
options: B) Add more weight and seal holes
quiz.explanation: High temperature means air is entering; adding weight and sealing holes restores anaerobic conditions.

quiz.q: How long can silage last if kept sealed and unopened?
quiz.explanation: Properly sealed silage can be stored for 2-3 years without significant quality loss.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to mark your bales to deter theft?
quiz.explanation: Painting or branding bales makes them easily identifiable if stolen and recovered.

quiz.q: Which animal is most likely to break into a hay store and cause damage?
quiz.explanation: Goats are strong and curious, often breaking fences to reach stored feed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gap between hay stacks and walls for inspection?
quiz.explanation: A 30 cm gap allows you to walk around and check for pests, moisture, and damage.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record the date you stored each batch of feed?
options: A) To know when to sell
B) To track age and use oldest first
quiz.explanation: Knowing storage dates helps you rotate stock and use older feed before it spoils.

quiz.q: What is a good way to keep the cover of a silage pit from blowing away?
quiz.explanation: Ropes, tires, and stones are all effective at holding down covers in windy conditions.

quiz.q: How can you tell if hay is too wet for storage?
options: A) It is light and fluffy
B) It heats up and smells musty
D) It is easy to stack
quiz.explanation: Wet hay heats up and develops a musty smell due to mold and bacterial activity.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a well-managed inventory?
options: A) You can feed more animals
B) You avoid running out of feed
quiz.explanation: Good inventory management ensures you have enough feed to last until the next harvest.
